boundary_rationale: This part opens on Babylon's own gods collapsing: “Bel bows down. Nebo stoops. Their idols are carried by animals, and on the livestock. The things that you carried around are heavy loads, a burden for the weary.” (web:Isa.46.1) sets the idols of Bel and Nebo onto pack animals as dead weight, their load named with the ordinary carrying-noun מַשָּׂ֖א לַעֲיֵפָֽה (oshb:Isa.46.1, byte tier) -- a burden common noun in this idol-procession scene, not a verse-initial oracle header of the massa series. The same noun recurs as the idols themselves cannot rescue what they carry: “They stoop and they bow down together. They could not deliver the burden, but they have gone into captivity.” (web:Isa.46.2), closing the tableau on their own captivity. A carry/bear catchword bridges into the next verse's divine address (web:Isa.46.3), which the row does not treat as reason enough to hold this tableau and that address in one unit, since web:Isa.46.3 turns the discourse from third-person description to a first-person vocative with a named addressee, the stronger seam signal here.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A rival reading merges this tableau with the divine carry-claim that follows at Isa.46.3-Isa.46.4, since the same carry/bear root spans both, but the fresh vocative address at Isa.46.3 is read as the stronger boundary signal.
literature_type_guess: third-person taunt-tableau of Babylon's collapsing idol-procession

boundary_rationale: A fresh vocative opens this row: “Listen to me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, that have been carried from their birth, that have been carried from the womb.” (web:Isa.46.3), שִׁמְע֤וּ אֵלַי֙ (oshb:Isa.46.3, byte tier), turning from the idols' own collapse (web:Isa.46.1-Isa.46.2) to Yahweh's own first-person carry-claim, “Even to old age I am he, and even to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear. Yes, I will carry, and will deliver.” (web:Isa.46.4) -- וַאֲנִ֣י אֶשָּׂ֔א (oshb:Isa.46.4, byte tier) answers the very carry/bear root that named the idols' load, a deliberate contrast rather than a seam. The comparison challenge “To whom will you compare me, and consider my equal, and compare me, as if we were the same?” (web:Isa.46.5) and the self-declaration “Remember the former things of old; for I am God, and there is no other. I am God, and there is none like me.” (web:Isa.46.9), אָנֹכִ֥י אֵל֙ וְאֵ֣ין ע֔וֹד (oshb:Isa.46.9, byte tier), carry the disputation forward through the appeal opening web:Isa.46.8 and the Cyrus prediction “I call a ravenous bird from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country. Yes, I have spoken. I will also bring it to pass. I have planned. I will also do it.” (web:Isa.46.11) with no fresh addressee onset at either point. The row closes on a second imperative address, “Listen to me, you stubborn-hearted, who are far from righteousness!” (web:Isa.46.12) -- שִׁמְע֥וּ אֵלַ֖י (oshb:Isa.46.12) -- matching the opening's שִׁמְע֤וּ אֵלַי֙ (oshb:Isa.46.3) at the accent-stripped tier and bracketing the whole disputation, before the closing promise “I bring my righteousness near. It is not far off, and my salvation will not wait. I will grant salvation to Zion, my glory to Israel.” (web:Isa.46.13), the row's own closing verse before a fresh address to a new addressee opens the following row at web:Isa.47.1.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A rival cut would open a fresh row at the appeal opening Isa.46.8 rather than reading it as bracketed inside the wider disputation running from Isa.46.3 to Isa.46.12.
literature_type_guess: divine incomparability disputation addressed to Jacob/Israel, closing on a promise of salvation to Zion

boundary_rationale: This row opens directly after the previous row's closing salvation promise (web:Isa.46.13) on a fresh imperative address to a new addressee: “Come down and sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon. Sit on the ground without a throne, daughter of the Chaldeans. For you will no longer be called tender and delicate.” (web:Isa.47.1), רְדִ֣י וּשְׁבִ֣י (oshb:Isa.47.1, byte tier), commanding personified Babylon down from her throne. The redeemer confession “Our Redeemer, Yahweh of Armies is his name, is the Holy One of Israel.” (web:Isa.47.4) -- גֹּאֲלֵ֕נוּ יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת שְׁמ֑וֹ קְד֖וֹשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל (oshb:Isa.47.4, byte tier) -- is a brief communal aside naming the book's qadosh-Israel title rather than a fresh address to Babylon, so the row holds it inside the surrounding sentence rather than opening its own unit. The matching imperative “Sit in silence, and go into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans. For you shall no longer be called the mistress of kingdoms.” (web:Isa.47.5) resumes the address to the same addressee named in web:Isa.47.1, continuing the same movement through Babylon's own boast, “You said, ‘I will be a princess forever,’ so that you didn’t lay these things to your heart, nor did you remember the results.” (web:Isa.47.7), the row's own closing verse before the pivot to a fresh summons formula at web:Isa.47.8.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A rival reading treats the daughter-of-Babylon address as one sustained unit through Isa.47.15, since the addressee stays the same across the chapter's 15 verses (sweep: 15 verses); this row reads the summons formula opening Isa.47.8 as a sufficient internal pivot for a cut there.

It won’t be a coal to warm at or a fire to sit by. The things that you labored in will be like this: those who have trafficked with you from your youth will each wander in his own way. There will be no one to save you.” (web:Isa.47.14-Isa.47.15), the row's own closing verses before the fresh summons formula opening the next row at web:Isa.48.1.

boundary_rationale: A fresh summons formula opens this row: “Hear this, house of Jacob, you who are called by the name of Israel, and have come out of the waters of Judah. I will not give my glory to another.” (web:Isa.48.11), the row's own closing verse before a second imperative vocative opens the next row at web:Isa.48.12.

boundary_rationale: A second imperative vocative opens this row after the self-interest close of the previous row (web:Isa.48.11): “Listen to me, O Jacob, and Israel my called: I am he. I am the first. I am also the last.” (web:Isa.48.12), שְׁמַ֤ע אֵלַי֙ יַֽעֲקֹ֔ב (oshb:Isa.48.12, byte tier), a singular address distinct from the plural summons that opened the earlier row at web:Isa.48.1. The self-declaration and creation claim carry into the assembly-summons “Assemble yourselves, all of you, and hear! Who among them has declared these things? He whom Yahweh loves will do what he likes to Babylon, and his arm will be against the Chaldeans.” (web:Isa.48.14), naming Yahweh's own action against Babylon and the Chaldeans. The sender clause “Come near to me and hear this: “From the beginning I have not spoken in secret; from the time that it happened, I was there.” Now the Lord Yahweh has sent me with his Spirit.” (web:Isa.48.16) -- וְעַתָּ֗ה אֲדֹנָ֧י יְהוִ֛ה שְׁלָחַ֖נִי וְרוּחֽוֹ (oshb:Isa.48.16, byte tier) -- names a first-person speaker the row does not attribute to a decided identity; the koh-amar formula “Yahweh, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, says: “I am Yahweh your God, who teaches you to profit, who leads you by the way that you should go.” (web:Isa.48.17), כֹּֽה אָמַ֧ר יְהוָ֛ה (oshb:Isa.48.17, byte tier), frames the teaching that follows as Yahweh's own, and the row closes on the lament “Oh that you had listened to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river and your righteousness like the waves of the sea. Your offspring also would have been as the sand and the descendants of your body like its grains. His name would not be cut off nor destroyed from before me.”” (web:Isa.48.18-Isa.48.19), the row's own closing verses before the bare departure imperative opening the next row at web:Isa.48.20.

boundary_rationale: A bare departure imperative opens this row with no hear-formula: “Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans! With the sound of joyful shouting announce this, tell it even to the end of the earth; say, “Yahweh has redeemed his servant Jacob!”” (web:Isa.48.20), צְא֣וּ מִבָּבֶל֮ בִּרְח֣וּ מִכַּשְׂדִּים֒ (oshb:Isa.48.20, byte tier), moving from the teaching lament closing the previous row at web:Isa.48.19 into an enacted proclamation. The same verse closes on a named referent for the servant word rather than the book's unnamed servant-figure crux: גָּאַ֥ל יְהוָ֖ה עַבְדּ֥וֹ יַעֲקֹֽב (oshb:Isa.48.20, byte tier), “Yahweh has redeemed his servant Jacob!” -- Jacob is the referent stated in the verse's own bytes. The wilderness memory “They didn’t thirst when he led them through the deserts. He caused the waters to flow out of the rock for them. He also split the rock and the waters gushed out.” (web:Isa.48.21) leads into the closing verdict, “There is no peace”, says Yahweh, “for the wicked.”” (web:Isa.48.22), אֵ֣ין שָׁל֔וֹם אָמַ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה לָרְשָׁעִֽים (oshb:Isa.48.22, byte tier), the row's own closing verse, ahead of a different frame opening at web:Isa.49.1.
